sources.claim: EL PAIS English (14 Apr 2025) reports the killing of Sara Millerey, a trans woman, in Bello, Antioquia: she was attacked in broad daylight, the assault was filmed and the video went viral on 5 April 2025, and she died of a second cardiac arrest at three the following afternoon, with no one arrested although police interrogated local residents; President Gustavo Petro asked authorities to investigate urgently and events were held in several cities to denounce transphobia. Hate killed 13 trans people in Colombia in the first quarter of 2025, and the article recalls earlier fatal attacks (gay men lured through an app and killed, a trans rough-sleeper stabbed while sleeping, others killed in their homes or in a hairdresser). It contains no Nariño-specific legal, enforcement or incident finding; for this record its value is national context.

The Guardian investigation (30 Jul 2024) documents armed groups in Caqueta department: three armed men told trans woman Tatiana Cespedes, 51, she had one week to leave town or be killed, and after hiding for a week she fled at night; 'social cleansing' flyers appeared on Caqueta streets and via WhatsApp naming 'faggots, lesbians and men and women who destroy homes' as legitimate military targets, a campaign by armed groups still operating despite the 2016 peace agreement. It reports eight trans women were killed in Colombia between February and April 2024 and 41 in 2023, and that discrimination limits trans women mainly to hairdressing or sex work. It contains no Nariño-specific finding; the national armed-group violence, threats and displacement pattern is the claim this record relies on.

This province has no province-specific law, ordinance or incident series in the audited record; what a trans visitor here stands under is the same national framework that binds every province. A leaked draft omnibus justice package from October 2025 (the '11th Judicial Package') would enable criminal charges against LGBT people across Turkiye - Human Rights Watch called it one of the most alarming rights rollbacks in decades - and it contains no province-specific provisions. The LGBTI+ association Kaos GL reported that in 2025 anti-LGBTI+ hostility became institutionalised as state policy under a 'Year of the Family' banner, with senior officials' rhetoric and instructions to public institutions creating a climate encouraging rights violations.

Because the surviving record is entirely national-level and carries no provincial breakdown, neither a more protective nor a more hostile local regime can be established for this province; the documented national picture applies here unchanged.
visible.tangentialFactors: The draft 11th Judicial Package's penalties for symbolic same-sex ceremonies (up to 4 years) and the nationwide 2025 'Year of the Family' hostility campaign shape police posture toward gender-nonconforming people here as in every other province, even before the amendments are enacted.

sources.claim: Human Rights Watch news release (29 Oct 2025) on the leaked '11th Judicial Package' draft omnibus law: would amend the Turkish penal and civil codes to criminalise behaviour deemed 'contrary to biological sex and general morality', criminalise taking part in a same-sex engagement or marriage ceremony (penalties up to 4 years in prison), raise the minimum age for gender-affirming health care including surgery from 18 to 25 with mandatory permanent infertility, and punish health professionals who perform such care - HRW calls it one of the most alarming rollbacks of LGBT rights in decades, and 15 Turkish LGBT groups plus the Turkish Medical Association oppose the draft.

Kaos GL report launch on the 2025 report 'A major siege against LGBTI+ people in 2025: Hostility turned into state policy': documents that anti-LGBTI+ hostility became institutionalised as explicit state policy, with senior officials' hate speech and instructions issued to public institutions under a 'Year of the Family' banner creating a climate that encouraged human-rights violations, and regulatory/supervisory bodies systematically restricting freedom of expression and artistic freedom; findings were presented by lawyer Kerem Dikmen at the launch.

visible.summary: Route-3 estimate, now carrying real sub-national evidence: the south-east's largest metropolis, with a conflict-era security legacy (state-of-emergency legacies, village-guard system, high police presence). On 14 September 2024 - the day of a national anti-LGBT "Great Family Gathering" - two men attacked two trans women with sharp objects in the Kayapınar district: Sudenaz Uran was killed at the scene and her friend was injured; the defendants recorded the killing and the recording entered the case file. On 19 December 2025 both were sentenced to aggravated life imprisonment for intentional killing of a woman - the strongest homicide-justice outcome in this country's record - though during the trial the Family and Social Services Ministry's application to intervene was accepted while the local bar association's LGBTI+ commission's was rejected, casting the state as guardian of "the family" rather than of the victim's community. Scored relative to the national score (0.15) for Turkey.
visible.tangentialFactors: The national "Year of the Family" hostility climate (presidency-centred; implemented through the family ministry, religious and broadcasting authorities) applies in this province as it does nationwide - a broad anti-LGBTI+ climate rather than a trans-specific local policy; no province-specific enforcement of the draft law is documented here yet.
visible.localsOnly: The local bar association's LGBTI+ commission's litigation role (its party application was rejected in the 2025 murder trial while the family ministry's was accepted) is resident and advocate-facing, not visitor-facing.
visible.outOfScopeNotes: General terrorism and crime advisories affect all travellers to this country regardless of identity; the 2025 draft judicial package's other measures (longer child sentences, online content removal) are not trans-specific. In this province specifically, the conflict-era security environment (state-of-emergency legacies, village-guard system, high police presence) affects everyone regardless of identity.

sources.claim: Human Rights Watch (29 October 2025): a leaked draft of Türkiye's 11th Judicial Package would amend penal-code article 225 to punish conduct 'contrary to biological sex' with up to 3 years in prison and would allow charges for anyone taking part in a same-sex engagement or marriage ceremony (up to 4 years) plus, under civil-code article 40, raise the minimum age for gender-affirming care from 18 to 25 with a permanent-infertility mandate (providers facing fines and up to 7 years, patients up to 3 years); 15 LGBT groups and the Turkish Medical Association objected and HRW calls for withdrawal. This is the national framework this province's record stands under; the article records no province-specific enforcement or incidents.

Kaos GL's LGBTI+ Human Rights Report 2025 ('A Major Siege', published 24 February 2026) finds hostility became explicit state policy in 2025 under 'Year of the Family' instructions, documenting six right-to-life violations including three hate-motivated killings with trans people most affected, 89 torture/ill-treatment violations (up from 51), and 313 right-to-liberty violations (about 2.5 times the previous year, mostly detentions); the state keeps no official hate-crime statistics, so data rely on media coverage. It is a national-level report and contains no province-specific detail.

sources.claim: Human Rights news release (29 October 2025): the leaked 11th Judicial Package omnibus draft law would amend the penal and civil codes to criminalise conduct deemed "contrary to biological sex and general morality" (up to three years), sharply restrict gender-affirming healthcare (minimum age 25, onerous eligibility conditions) and allow criminal charges against both trans people and the professionals providing their care; the government's stated justification is protecting "the family" and "public morals"; the package also carries unrelated measures such as longer child sentences and online-content removal.

Wikipedia's Turkey country overview supplies the national framework a visitor to an interior province like Düzce stands under: consensual same-sex activity has been decriminalised since the 1858 Ottoman penal code, and transgender people have been able to change their legal gender since 1988, but Turkish marriage law still gives same-sex relationships no legal recognition and offers no civil unions, domestic partnerships or joint adoption, while no comprehensive law bans discrimination on sexual orientation or gender identity and LGBTQ people are barred from open military service. It also tracks the criminalisation push the record's HRW source describes: in early 2026 Turkish media reported the government was considering legislation criminalising public advocacy of 'behaviour contrary to biological sex', and that provision was ultimately not included in that year's judicial reform package; Pride events and LGBTQ gatherings were repeatedly disallowed in 2024 and 2025 with police detaining participants, per Amnesty International. The page carries no Düzce-specific content, so it stands only as the framework against which the record's national-score-derived model estimate for Düzce sits.
